messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir, a 42‑year‑old Indian American tax inspector, recalls the moment that turned his life from routine to haunting with a clarity that feels more cinematic than lived. He was driving home after a long day of filing returns, when a delivery truck, swerving to avoid a sudden pothole, spun and collided with his sedan. The crash left a fellow driver severely injured, and Amir was immediately flooded with a chorus of sound—the crunch of metal, the scream of a passenger, and the hiss of air‑bag inflation. He was later diagnosed with post‑traumatic stress disorder, scoring 72 on the PCL‑5, and his symptoms have grown entrenched over the past two years. The images of cars smashing together have become a constant, invisible trigger. Whenever Amir’s supervisor shows a slide of traffic statistics on the office screen, he feels the memory flash back so vividly that he involuntarily withdraws his hand from the keyboard, forcing a pause in his work. This withdrawal is not merely a reflex; the trigger directly leads him into his self‑punishing thoughts. He tells himself that he deserves to suffer because of what happened, that he should have protected the other driver, and that life is unforgivable. Those thoughts, in turn, deepen his sense of humiliation and reinforce his conviction that he has failed. He has learned to suppress any conversation about the crash, hoping that not thinking about it will make the memory fade, but the very act of trying to push the images away only amplifies their presence. The cycle of trigger, punishment thinking, and heightened shame is so relentless that Amir often avoids even looking at news reports of car accidents while on his commute, and he has begun to skip over traffic updates that appear in his tax‑audit briefing videos. Each avoidance tactic feeds back into the trigger loop, making him more sensitive to the same images he tried to escape. Amir’s recollection of the day is fragmentary. Some moments—such as the sudden jolt of the car and the scream—are etched in his mind with crystalline clarity, while other parts blur into nothingness. He often hears, in his head, the same radio chatter he heard that day, as if the auditory cues are replaying the trauma in real time. He feels as though he is only remembering bits of what happened and that the rest is missing. This sense of an incomplete picture is not a passive feeling; his humiliation and belief that the world no longer makes sense make him question the reliability of the memory itself. In the quiet moments at home, he tries to piece together the timeline, but the gaps only widen his fear that he may have misjudged what he should have done. The way his self‑punishing thoughts shape how he recalls the event—blurring some parts and sharpening others—feeds directly into his distorted appraisal of the world and his role in it. Over the months, these patterns have carved a niche in Amir’s daily routine. When he hears a car honk outside the office, his mind rushes to the crash, and he automatically thinks, “I should have been more careful.” That thought, coupled with the feeling that he has disgraced himself, pulls him further into shame, which, in turn, sharpens the images whenever he sees a car crash or a funeral notice. He now avoids family gatherings that include funeral urns, fearing that the sight of a gravesite will bring back the memory and the accompanying humiliation. His marriage has strained; he has stopped sharing his thoughts with his wife, fearing she will see him as weak. He has even begun to question whether his job, which requires him to review and analyze financial reports—often containing numbers that look like car registration plates—has become a constant source of trigger. Amir finally decided to seek help after a particularly harrowing night. While scrolling through a memorial page on social media, a photograph of a burial plot appeared in his feed. The image sent a shockwave of guilt and the feeling that he had abandoned his role as a protector. He realized that the self‑disciplining thoughts were no longer just internal monologues but were actively shaping his reality, making his days feel like a living nightmare. He is terrified that the cycle will continue to erode his sense of self and that his career might suffer if he cannot manage the triggers. Yet, he also holds a quiet hope that by breaking the loop, he can reclaim his life, regain trust in himself, and protect his loved ones from the weight of his own guilt.
